groups.title: Redis & Caching
groups.question: Explain how you would use Redis to make a Node.js API faster.

followUps.Cache-Aside Pattern with Redis: What goes wrong with cache-aside if you have no TTL or invalidation plan?
followUps.Redis Data Structures: Pick one Redis data structure beyond plain strings and explain a problem it solves well.

evidence.text: The app checks the cache first; on a miss it reads the database, stores the result in the cache and returns it.
Without a TTL or invalidation on writes, the cache keeps serving old data after the database changes.
Setting a TTL and deleting or updating the key when the data changes keeps it fresh enough.

notEnough: Only saying cache with Redis without explaining the miss path or invalidation.

evidence.text: Redis has structures like hashes, lists, sets and sorted sets, each with atomic operations.
The answer picks one and explains a real use, for example a sorted set for a leaderboard or a set for unique visitors.

notEnough: Only listing data structure names without explaining a use for one.

groups.title: Background Jobs with BullMQ
groups.question: Walk through how you move slow work out of the request path with a job queue.

followUps.Job Queues & Workers: Why should an endpoint enqueue a 30-second task instead of doing it before responding?
followUps.Job Retries & Dead-Letter Queues: Why should failed jobs end up in a dead-letter queue instead of being dropped?

evidence.text: The endpoint puts a job in the queue and answers right away, and a separate worker process does the slow work.
Holding the request open for 30 seconds ties up resources, risks timeouts, and loses the work if the connection drops.

notEnough: Only saying use a queue without explaining why the request shouldn't wait.

evidence.text: Failed jobs are retried a set number of times with backoff, so temporary failures fix themselves.
Jobs that still fail go to a dead-letter queue instead of being dropped.
There they can be inspected, fixed and replayed, so no work is silently lost.

notEnough: Only saying jobs are retried without explaining what happens after the last failure.

groups.title: Performance Profiling
groups.question: Explain how you find out why a Node.js service is slow or using too much memory.

followUps.Profiling with --prof & Clinic.js: How would you use a profiler or flame graph to find what is eating CPU time?
followUps.Detecting & Fixing Memory Leaks: How would you track down a memory leak that only shows up after days of uptime?

evidence.text: A CPU profiler, like --prof, --cpu-prof or Clinic, samples where the process spends its time.
In a flame graph, the widest bars are the functions using the most CPU, which is where to look first.
Profiling should run under realistic load, so the hot paths show up.

notEnough: Only naming profiling tools without explaining how to read the result.

evidence.text: A leak shows as memory that keeps growing over time and isn't released by garbage collection.
Comparing heap snapshots taken some time apart shows which objects keep growing and what is holding on to them.
Common causes are growing caches or maps, forgotten listeners and timers, and closures keeping large objects alive.

notEnough: Only saying use a heap snapshot without explaining how to find the leak.

groups.title: Resource Pooling
groups.question: Explain how you manage connections to databases and caches under heavy load.

followUps.Database Connection Pool Tuning: What happens when a database pool is too large, and what happens when it is too small?
followUps.Redis Connection Management: Why should a service share one Redis client instead of creating one per request?

evidence.text: Too small a pool makes requests wait for a free connection even when the database has capacity.
Too large a pool, multiplied by every instance, can exceed the database's connection limit and slow it down with too many parallel queries.

notEnough: Only saying tune the pool size without explaining what goes wrong at each extreme.

evidence.text: A Redis client keeps one connection that can handle many commands, so one shared client serves all requests.
Creating a client per request opens and closes connections constantly, adds latency and can exhaust Redis's connection limit.

notEnough: Only saying reuse the client without explaining the cost of one per request.
